In the theory of [[formal language]]s, the '''interchange lemma''' states a necessary condition for a language to be [[context-free languages|context-free]], just like the [[pumping lemma for context-free languages]].

It states that for every context-free language <math>L</math> there is a <math>c>0</math> such that for all <math>n\geq m\geq 2</math> for any collection of length <math>n</math> words <math>R\subset L</math> there is a <math>Z=\{z_1,\ldots,z_k\}\subset R</math> with <math>k\ge |R|/(cn^2)</math>, and decompositions <math>z_i=w_ix_iy_i</math> such that each of <math>|w_i|</math>, <math>|x_i|</math>, <math>|y_i|</math> is independent of <math>i</math>, moreover, <math>m/2<|x_i|\leq m</math>, and the words <math>w_ix_jy_i</math> are in <math>L</math> for every <math>i</math> and <math>j</math>.

The first application of the interchange lemma was to show that the set of repetitive strings (i.e., strings of the form <math>xyyz</math> with <math>|y|>0</math>) over an alphabet of three or more characters is not context-free.
